newsitem.title: BELGIUM: CL Belgium now estimates 3.5 bln bfr stolen.
newsitem.headline: CL Belgium now estimates 3.5 bln bfr stolen.

text.p: Credit Lyonnais Belgium SA, the Belgian banking unit of French group Credit Lyonnais, said on Friday the estimate of funds allegedly stolen from the Belgian bank by a single former employee was now 3.5 billion francs.
Initially it had said 850 million francs had allegedly been stolen by the senior employee.
CLB said in a statement, "the general inspectorate of the bank has found that the amount illegally transferred by the said employee is around 3.5 billion Belgian francs."

The employee, a woman in CLB's Ghent office, is suspected of theft and forgery. Her husband, a businessman and chairman of a Belgian soccer team, has also been arrested. He is suspected of receiving stolen goods

The bank believed that it had been the victim of an international, well-organised fraud ring. CLB said the husband, who mainly benefitted from the alleged theft, was part of an "international ring of fraudsters."
CLB said "the operation" affected only the bank's own funds and not those of clients. It said the funds transferred and the assets belonging to the pair had already been blocked.
"For the surplus - the sums which eventually will not be recovered - the bank is largely covered by insurance policies," it said.
CLB chief executive officer Philippe Cloes said on Thursday after reports of the alleged theft that there would be no impact on 1996 earnings.
In 1995 CLB earned a 628 million franc profit.
He said on Thursday the woman had confessed to police that she stole 850 million francs.

Asked how an employee could steal such a large amount -- bigger than the bank's 1995 earnings -- Cloes said on Thursday: "Billions of francs move around every day in our bank. If one steals 20 million once a month, you don't see it."

"The lady had been with us for 30 years, we had absolute confidence in her." He said she probably started diverting funds in a limited way in 1992, but that in recent months the amounts had become bigger.
For CLB, which in 1995 suffered from negative press coverage of financial problems at its French parent company, the theft is another blow to its image.

CLB is a relatively small player in Belgian banking. At the end of June 1996 it had total assets of 547 billion francs, about a 10th of those of market leader Generale Bank. But its aggressive marketing policy and sharp pricing make it one of the most high-profile players in the industry.
